{{short description|Neighborhoods in New York City}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=August 2024}} {{Infobox Chinese | title = Chinatowns in Queens | pic = Main St Northern Bl td (2022-04-22) 01.jpg | piccap = Intersection of [[Main Street (Queens)|Main Street]] and [[Northern Blvd]] in Flushing Chinatown | picsize = 300px | type = [[Neighborhoods in Queens|Neighborhood of New York City]] | s = 皇后区唐人街 | t = 皇后區唐人街 | showflag = pj | p = Huánghòu-qū Tángrén-jiē | poj = Hông-hiō-khu Tn̂g-lâng-koe | tl = Hông-hiō-khu Tn̂g-lâng-kue | phfs = Vòng-hiu-khî Thòng-nyìn-kâi | w = | mi = | gr = | tp = | j = Wong4 Hau6 Keoi1 Tong4 Jan4 Gaai1 | y = | ci = | h = fongˇ heu kiˊ tongˇ nginˇ gieˊ }} There are multiple [[Chinatowns in the United States|Chinatowns]] in the [[borough (New York City)|borough]] of [[Queens]] in [[New York City]]. The original Queens Chinatown emerged in [[Flushing, Queens|Flushing]], initially as a satellite of the original [[Chinatown, Manhattan|Manhattan Chinatown]], before evolving its own identity, surpassing in scale the original Manhattan Chinatown, and subsequently, in turn, spawning its own satellite Chinatowns in [[Elmhurst, Queens|Elmhurst]], [[Corona, Queens|Corona]], and eastern Queens. As of 2023, illegal Chinese immigration to [[Chinese people in New York City|New York]] has accelerated, and its Flushing neighborhood has become the present-day global epicenter receiving Chinese immigration as well as the international control center directing such migration.{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/11/24/us/politics/china-migrants-us-border.html|title=Growing Numbers of Chinese Migrants Are Crossing the Southern Border|first=Eileen | last = Sullivan|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=November 24, 2023|access-date=November 24, 2023|quote=Most who have come to the United States in the past year were middle-class adults who have headed to New York after being released from custody. New York has been a prime destination for migrants from other nations as well, particularly Venezuelans, who rely on the city’s resources, including its shelters. But few of the Chinese migrants are staying in the shelters. Instead, they are going where Chinese citizens have gone for generations: Flushing, Queens. Or to some, the Chinese Manhattan...“New York is a self-sufficient Chinese immigrants community,” said the Rev. Mike Chan, the executive director of the Chinese Christian Herald Crusade, a faith-based group in the neighborhood.}} As of 2024, a significant new wave of [[Islam in China|Chinese Muslims]] are fleeing [[religious persecution]] in northwestern China’s [[Xinjiang|Xinjiang Province]] and seeking [[religious freedom]] in New York,{{cite web|url= https://www.cnn.com/2024/05/15/americas/new-york-city-chinese-migrants-flushing-intl-latam/index.html|title= Caught between China and the US, asylum seekers live in limbo in New York City|author1=Tara John | author2= Yong Xiong |publisher=[[CNN]]|date=May 17, 2024|access-date=June 9, 2024}} and concentrating in Queens. == Context == The [[New York metropolitan area]] is home to the largest ethnic Chinese population outside Asia, comprising an estimated 893,697 uniracial individuals as of 2017,{{cite web|url=https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/17_1YR/S0201/330M400US408/popgroup~016|title=SELECTED POPULATION PROFILE IN THE UNITED STATES 2017 American Community Survey 1-Year Estimates New York-Newark, NY-NJ-CT-PA CSA Chinese alone|publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]|access-date=January 27, 2019|archive-url=https://archive.today/20200214002005/https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/17_1YR/S0201/330M400US408/popgroup~016|archive-date=February 14, 2020|url-status=dead}} including at least 12 Chinatowns - six{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/06/24/nyregion/asian-new-yorkers-asian-new-yorkers-seek-power-to-match-surging-numbers.html |title=Asian New Yorkers Seek Power to Match Numbers |first=Kirk | last = Semple |newspaper=The New York Times |date=June 23, 2011 |access-date=2014-10-03}} (or nine, including the emerging Chinatowns in [[Corona, Queens|Corona]] and [[Whitestone, Queens|Whitestone]], [[Queens]],{{cite journal|url=http://geographyplanning.buffalostate.edu/MSG%202002/13_McGlinn.pdf |title=Beyond Chinatown: Dual Immigration and the Chinese Population of Metropolitan New York City, 2000 |first=Lawrence A. | last = McGlinn |journal=Middle States Geographer |year=2002 |volume=35 |issue=1153 |pages=110–119 | publisher = Middle States Division of the Association of American Geographers |access-date=3 October 2014 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121029075400/http://geographyplanning.buffalostate.edu/MSG%202002/13_McGlinn.pdf |archive-date=29 October 2012}} and [[East Harlem, Manhattan]]) in [[New York City]] proper, and one each in [[Nassau County, New York|Nassau County]], [[Long Island]]; [[Cherry Hill, New Jersey|Cherry Hill]], [[Edison, New Jersey|Edison]], [[New Jersey]]; and [[Parsippany-Troy Hills, New Jersey]], not to mention fledgling ethnic Chinese enclaves emerging throughout the New York City metropolitan area. [[Chinese Americans]], as a whole, have had a significant tenure in New York City. The first [[Chinese people|Chinese]] immigrants came to [[Lower Manhattan]] around 1870, looking for the "golden" opportunities America had to offer.{{cite web |url=http://www.ny.com/articles/chinatown.html|title=The History of New York's Chinatown|last=Waxman|first=Sarah |publisher=ny.com |access-date=2014-10-03}} By 1880, the enclave around [[Five Points, Manhattan|Five Points]] was estimated to have from 200 to as many as 1,100 members. However, the [[Chinese Exclusion Act]], which went into effect in 1882, caused an abrupt decline in the number of Chinese who immigrated to New York and the rest of the United States. Later, in 1943, the Chinese were given a small quota, and the community's population gradually increased until 1968, when the quota was lifted and the Chinese American population skyrocketed. In the past few years, the [[Cantonese]] dialect that has dominated the Chinatowns for decades is being rapidly swept aside by [[Standard Chinese|Mandarin Chinese]], the national language of China and the [[lingua franca]] of most of the latest [[Chinese immigrants]].{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/10/22/nyregion/22chinese.html |title=In Chinatown, Sound of the Future Is Mandarin |date=October 21, 2009 |access-date=2011-06-29 | work=The New York Times | first=Kirk | last=Semple}} ===Citywide demographics=== {{See also|List of U.S. cities with significant Chinese-American book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5PSYZMs8TzEC&q=fort+lee+koreatown+pyong+min&pg=PA237|title=Asian Americans: Contemporary Trends and Issues Second Edition, Edited by Pyong Gap Min|publisher=Pine Forge Press - An Imprint of Sage Publications, Inc.|year=2006|access-date=2010-11-08|isbn=978-1-4129-0556-5}} in [[Flushing, Queens|Flushing]], is one of the largest and fastest-growing ethnic [[Chinese people|Chinese]] [[enclave]]s outside Asia, as well as within New York City itself. Flushing Chinatown is in [[Main Street (Queens)|Main Street]] and the area to its west, particularly along [[Roosevelt Avenue]], has become the primary nexus of Flushing Chinatown. However, Chinatown continues to expand southeastward along [[Kissena Boulevard]] and northward beyond [[Northern Boulevard]]. The [[Flushing–Main Street station (IRT Flushing Line)|Flushing–Main Street station]] is the busiest [[New York City Subway]] station outside Manhattan. The Flushing Chinatown houses over 30,000 individuals born in China alone, the largest Chinatown by this metric outside Asia, the largest and fastest-growing Chinatown in the world, and one of the world's busiest [[pedestrian]] intersections.{{cite web|url=http://www.businessinsider.com/i-ate-my-way-through-flushing-queens-and-now-i-get-why-its-the-bigger-and-better-chinatown-2015-5 |title=This is what it's like in one of the biggest and fastest growing Chinatowns in the world |first=Melia | last = Robinson |work=Business Insider |date=May 27, 2015 |access-date=July 23, 2017}} Flushing is undergoing rapid [[gentrification]] by Chinese transnational entities.{{cite news |url=https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2020/aug/13/flushing-queens-gentrification-luxury-developments |title='Not what it used to be': in New York, Flushing's Asian residents brace against gentrification |first=Sarah |last = Ngu |newspaper=[[The Guardian US]] |date=January 29, 2021 |access-date=August 13, 2020 |quote=The three developers have stressed in public hearings that they are not outsiders to Flushing, which is 69% Asian. 'They’ve been here, they live here, they work here, they’ve invested here,' said Ross Moskowitz, an attorney for the developers at a different public hearing in February...Tangram Tower, a luxury mixed-use development built by F&T. Last year, prices for two-bedroom apartments started at $1.15m...The influx of transnational capital and rise of luxury developments in Flushing has displaced longtime immigrant residents and small business owners, as well as disrupted its cultural and culinary landscape. These changes follow the familiar script of gentrification, but with a change of actors: it is Chinese American developers and wealthy Chinese immigrants who are gentrifying this working-class neighborhood, which is majority Chinese.}} ===History=== ====Before Chinatown==== {{Main|Flushing, Queens#History}} In 1645, Flushing was established by [[Dutch colonial empire|Dutch]] settlers on the eastern bank of [[Flushing Creek]] under charter of the [[Dutch West India Company]] and was part of the [[New Netherland|New Netherland colony]]. The settlement was named after the city of [[Flushing, Netherlands|Vlissingen]], in the southwestern Netherlands, the main [[port]] of the company; Flushing is the historic [[anglicization]] of the Dutch name of that town. In 1664, the English took control of [[New Amsterdam]], ending Dutch control of the colony, and renamed it the [[Province of New York]]. When Queens County was established in 1683, the "Town of Flushing" was one of the original five [[Town (New York)|towns]] which comprised the county.{{cite web |url=http://www.bklyn-genealogy-info.com/Map/5.Bor.Q.Rich.html |title=Before the Five Borough City:Queens |access-date=2014-10-03 |archive-date=2012-03-14 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120314044721/http://www.bklyn-genealogy-info.com/Map/5.Bor.Q.Rich.html |url-status=dead }} This later map shows former boundaries of the Town of Flushing. The map does not show the towns that were part of Queens and are now part of Nassau. Many historical references to Flushing are to this town, bounded from Newtown on the west by Flushing Creek (now often called the [[Flushing River]]), from [[Jamaica, Queens|Jamaica]] on the south by the "hills"—that is, the terminal [[moraine]] left by the last glacier, and from [[Hempstead, New York|Hempstead]] on the east by what later became the [[Nassau County, New York|Nassau County]] line. The town was dissolved in 1898 when Queens became a borough of New York City, and the term "Flushing" today usually refers to a much smaller area, including the former Village of Flushing and the areas immediately to the east and south. It was later settled by multiple ethnicities, including people of European, Hispanic, South-West Asian, African, and eventually East Asian ancestry. ====Emergence as Little Taipei / Little Taiwan==== In the 1970s, a Chinese community established a foothold in Flushing, whose demographic constituency had been predominantly white, interspersed with a small [[Japanese people|Japanese]] community. This wave of immigrants from [[Taiwan]] were the first to arrive and developed Flushing's Chinatown. It was known as '''Little Taipei''' ({{lang|zh|小台北}}) or '''Little Taiwan''' ({{lang|zh|小台灣}}). Many who arrived were the descendants of former soldiers and political supporters of [[Chiang Kai-shek]] and the [[Kuomindang|Chinese Nationalist Party]], which had lost the war against the [[Chinese Communist Party]], and established themselves in Taiwan. Along with immigrants from Taiwan at this time, a large [[Korean diaspora|South Korean]] population has also called Flushing home. Before the 1970s, [[Cantonese people|Cantonese immigrants]] had vastly dominated Chinese immigration to New York City; however, during the 1970s, the Taiwanese immigrants were the first wave of Chinese immigrants who spoke Mandarin rather than Cantonese to arrive in New York City. Due to the dominance of Cantonese-speaking immigrants, who were largely working-class in [[Chinatown, Manhattan|Manhattan's Chinatown]] ({{zh|c=紐約華埠|j=Nau2 Joek3 Waa4 Fau6}}), as well as the language barrier and poor housing conditions there, Taiwanese immigrants, who were more likely to have attained higher [[educational standards]] and [[socioeconomic status]], could not relate to Manhattan's Chinatown, and chose to settle in Flushing instead. As the Taiwanese population grew, a Flushing Chinatown was created with a higher [[standard of living]] and better housing conditions. ====Mandarin Town, Flushing==== [[File:Flushing, After the Rain.jpg|thumb|right|250px|The intersection of Main St and Roosevelt Ave after an early morning rainstorm.]] Over the years, many new non-Cantonese ethnic Chinese immigrants from different regions and [[provinces of China]] started to arrive in New York City and settled in Flushing through word of mouth. This led to the creation of a more '''Mandarin-speaking Chinatown''' or '''Mandarin Town''' that gradually replaced '''Little Taipei'''. This wave of immigrants spoke Mandarin and various regional/provincial dialects. The early 1990s into the 2000s brought a wave of [[Fuzhounese Americans]] and [[Wenzhounese]] immigrants. Like the Taiwanese, they faced cultural and communication problems in Manhattan's predominantly Cantonese-speaking Chinatown and settled in Flushing as well as [[Elmhurst, Queens]], which also has a significant Mandarin-speaking population. Flushing's Chinese population became very diverse over the next few decades as people from different provinces started to arrive, infusing their varied languages and cultures into this new "Chinatown."{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=MR4iVnvulMQC&pg=PA158|title=New immigrants in New York|first=Nancy|last=Foner|publisher=[[Columbia University Press]]|year=2001|pages=158–161|isbn=978-0-231-12414-0}}{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5PSYZMs8TzEC&q=Flushing+Chinatown+Little+Taiwan&pg=PA134 |title=Asian Americans: contemporary trends ... – Google Books |isbn=9781412905565 |access-date=August 28, 2011|last1=Min |first1=Pyong Gap |year=2006 |publisher=Pine Forge Press }}{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZcBxKK0cljcC&q=Flushing+Chinatown+Little+Taiwan&pg=PA190 |title=Chinatown: The Socioeconomic ... – Google Books |date=January 24, 1995 |isbn=9781439904176 |access-date=August 28, 2011|last1=Zhou |first1=Min |publisher=Temple University Press }}{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NagJFMxtkAcC&q=Flushing+Chinatown+Little+Taiwan&pg=PA104 |title=Still the golden door: the Third ... – Google Books |first=David M. | last = Reimers |year=1992 |publisher=Columbia University Press |isbn=9780231076814 |access-date=December 15, 2011}} Due to the increased opening of Mainland China, there has also been a growing [[Northern China|Northern Chinese]] population in Flushing. Flushing and its Chinatown abuts the rapidly growing [[Koreatown, Long Island|Long Island Koreatown]] as well.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=5PSYZMs8TzEC&q=fort+lee+koreatown+pyong+min&pg=PA237|title=Asian Americans: Contemporary Trends and Issues Second Edition, Edited by Pyong Gap Min|publisher=Pine Forge Press - An Imprint of Sage Publications, Inc|year=2006|access-date=2013-01-11|isbn=9781412905565}} ===Chinese demographic=== The intersection of Main Street and Roosevelt Avenue, in the heart of the Chinatown neighborhood, hosts a large concentration of Chinese businesses, including Chinese restaurants. Chinese-owned businesses in particular dominate the area along Main Street and the blocks west of it, while Korean businesses are found in a substantial number east of Main Street and east of the Flushing Chinatown, on Union Street. The majority of signs and advertisements of stores in the area have become Chinese. Ethnic Chinese constitute an increasingly dominant proportion of the Asian population and as well as of the overall population in Flushing. Consequently, Flushing's Chinatown has grown rapidly enough to become the largest Chinatown outside Asia. The Flushing Chinatown has surpassed the original Manhattan Chinatown in size. As of 2023, [[Chinese emigration|illegal Chinese immigration]] to [[Chinese people in New York City|New York]], and especially to Queens and its [[Flushing Chinatown]], has accelerated. Flushing has become the present-day global epicenter receiving Chinese immigration as well as the international control center directing such migration. A 1986 estimate by the Flushing Chinese Business Association approximated 60,000 Chinese in Flushing alone.{{cite web|url=http://qcpages.qc.edu/Asian_American_Center/research_papers/aacre15.html|access-date=2010-03-29|title=Chinese in Chinatown and Flushing|author=Hsiang-shui Chen|archive-date=2011-07-20|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110720033810/http://qcpages.qc.edu/Asian_American_Center/research_papers/aacre15.html|url-status=dead}} By 1990, Asians constituted 41% of the population of the core area of Flushing, with Chinese in turn representing 41% of the Asian population. However, ethnic Chinese are constituting an increasingly dominant proportion of the Asian population as well as of the overall population in Flushing and its Chinatown. High rates of both legal{{cite web|url=https://www.dhs.gov/files/statistics/publications/LPR11.shtm|title=Yearbook of Immigration Statistics: 2011 Supplemental Table 2|publisher=U.S. Department of Homeland Security|access-date=2012-09-18}}{{cite web|url=https://www.dhs.gov/files/statistics/publications/LPR10.shtm|title=Yearbook of Immigration Statistics: 2010 Supplemental Table 2|publisher=U.S. Department of Homeland Security|access-date=2012-09-18}} and illegal{{cite news|url=http://articles.nydailynews.com/2011-05-09/news/29541916_1_illegal-chinese-immigrants-qm2-queen-mary|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120623083222/http://articles.nydailynews.com/2011-05-09/news/29541916_1_illegal-chinese-immigrants-qm2-queen-mary|url-status=dead|archive-date=June 23, 2012|title=Malaysian man smuggled illegal Chinese immigrants into Brooklyn using Queen Mary 2: authorities|first=John | last = Marzulli|work = NY Daily News |date=May 9, 2011|access-date=2012-09-18|location=New York}} immigration from [[Mainland China]] continue to spur the ongoing rise of the ethnic Chinese population in Flushing, as in all of New York City's Chinatowns. [[File:Bank of China on Main Street in Flushing.jpg|thumb|250px|[[Bank of China]] on Main Street in Flushing]] Flushing's Chinatown ranks as New York City's largest Chinese community with 33,526 Chinese, up from 17,363, a 93% increase. The [[Chinatown, Brooklyn|Brooklyn Chinatown]] is the second-largest Chinatown of NYC with 34,218 Chinese residents, up from 19,963 in 2000, a 71% increase. As for Manhattan's Chinatown, its Chinese population declined by 17%, from 34,554 to 28,681 since 2000, to become the third-largest.{{cite news|url=http://www.nydailynews.com/changing-chinatowns-move-manhattan-sunset-park-home-chinese-nyc-article-1.948028|title=The changing Chinatowns: Move over Manhattan, Sunset Park now home to most Chinese in NYC|first=Daniel | last = Beekman|newspaper=NY Daily News|date=2011-08-05|access-date=2012-09-18}} Of all the Chinatowns of New York City, the Flushing Chinatown is also the most diverse, with large populations of Chinese groups from various regions of [[Mainland China]] and [[Taiwan]]. The [[Northeast China|Northeastern Chinese immigrants]] are increasingly becoming the largest Chinese group in Flushing.{{Cite web | https://medium.com/flushing/flushing-where-mainland-chinese-immigrants-are-moving-in-42156f62943a| title = Flushing, N.Y. : Where Mainland Chinese Immigrants Are Moving In | author = Muyao Shen | work this is comparable to how [[Shenzhen, China]] as a migrant city is largely populated by residents from almost every part of China and Taiwan but because it is located in [[Guangdong province]] it still retains a limited number of the original local Cantonese and Hakka speaking populations mixed in. In many ways, this can be considered as '''Little Shenzhen'''(小深圳) despite not officially having this title or not being recognized by media.{{cite web |last=Zhang |first=Emily |date=June 18, 2021 |url=https://storymaps.arcgis.com/stories/c8373fd7f8c84512848032f1e1ab449e |title=Shenzhen Part 2 |access-date=June 1, 2026}}{{cite web |last=Yu |first=Zhang |date=August 1, 2026 |url=https://www.eyeshenzhen.com/content/2025-08/01/content_31648839.htm |title='SZ second generation' reshaping narratives of Shenzhen |access-date=June 1, 2026}}{{cite web |date=April 21, 2025 |url=https://chinapartnership.org/blog/2025/04/shenzhen-working-migrants/ |title=Shenzhen: Working Migrants |website=China Partnership |access-date=June 1, 2026}}{{cite news |last1=Main |first1=Emma |last2=Zuoin |first2=Mandy |date=May 26, 2026 |url=https://www.scmp.com/economy/china-economy/article/3354772/china-now-home-more-people-over-65-children-official-survey-finds?module=perpetual_scroll_1_RM&pgtype=article |title=China now home to more people over 65 than children, official survey finds |work=South China Morning Post |access-date=June 1, 2026}} ===Streetscape=== {{Wide image|Flushing Queens May 2015 2.jpg|800px|3=
The busy intersection of [[Main Street (Queens)|Main Street]], [[Kissena Boulevard]], and 41st Avenue in the Flushing Chinatown ({{lang|zh|法拉盛華埠}}), the largest and fastest-growing Chinatown in the world, and one of the world's busiest [[pedestrian]] intersections. The segment of Main Street between Kissena Boulevard and [[Roosevelt Avenue]], punctuated by the [[Long Island Rail Road]] [[Trestle bridge|trestle]] overpass, represents the cultural heart of Flushing Chinatown. Queens' rapidly growing [[Chinese Americans in New York City|Chinese American]] population was approaching 250,000 in 2016,{{cite web|url=https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/16_1YR/S0201/0500000US36081/popgroup~016|title=Selected Population Profile in the United States - 2016 American Community Survey 1-Year Estimates Queens County, New York Chinese alone|publisher=[[United States Census Bureau]]|access-date=December 28, 2017|archive-url=https://archive.today/20200214004137/https://factfinder.census.gov/bkmk/table/1.0/en/ACS/16_1YR/S0201/0500000US36081/popgroup~016|archive-date=February 14, 2020|url-status=dead}} the [[List of U.S. cities with significant Chinese-American populations#New York City boroughs|highest of any municipality in the United States]] other than New York City overall. As of 2023, [[Chinese emigration|illegal Chinese immigration]] to [[Chinese people in New York City|New York]], and especially to Queens and its [[Flushing Chinatown]], has accelerated.
|dir=rtl}} ===Culture=== Flushing Chinatown now rivals Manhattan's Chinatown as a center of [[Chinese culture]]{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/10/22/nyregion/22chinese.html|title=In Chinatown, Sound of the Future Is Mandarin|date=October 21, 2009|access-date=April 6, 2010 | work=The New York Times | first=Kirk | last=Semple}} and has been called the "Chinese [[Times Square]]" or the "Chinese Manhattan".{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2014/10/05/realestate/downtown-flushing-where-asian-cultures-thrive.html|title=Downtown Flushing: Where Asian Cultures Thrive|first=Vera|last=Haller|newspaper=The New York Times|date=October 1, 2014|access-date=July 30, 2017}} The [[Chinese New Year|Lunar New Year]] Parade has become a growing annual celebration of [[Chinese New Year]]. More and larger [[Chinese supermarket]]s are locating and selling a diverse array of Chinese food and ingredient selections in Flushing, the largest of which include [[Hong Kong Supermarket]] and New York Supermarket, which also happen to be rapidly growing [[Chinese American]] chain supermarkets.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=_4QcI7q4CG0C&q=Hong+Kong+Supermarket+Flushing&pg=PA97 |title=Queens: What to Do, Where to Go (and How Not to Get Lost) in New York's Undiscovered Borough |first=Ellen |last=Freudenheim |date=31 October 2006 |publisher=Macmillan |isbn=9780312358181 |access-date=December 15, 2011}}{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YjJSI1L5QCQC&q=Hong+Kong+Supermarket+Flushing&pg=PA79 |title=Nosh New York: The Food Lover's Guide to New York City's Most Delicious Neighborhoods |first=Myra |last=Alperson |publisher=Macmillan |date=September 20, 2003 |isbn=9780312304171 |access-date=July 30, 2017}}{{cite web|last=Greenhouse |first=Steven |url=http://cityroom.blogs.nytimes.com/2008/12/09/supermarket-to-pay-back-wages-and-overtime/ |title=Supermarket to Pay Back Wages and Overtime – NYTimes.com |publisher=Cityroom.blogs.nytimes.com |date=December 9, 2008 |access-date=July 30, 2017}} The segment of Main Street between Roosevelt Avenue and Kissena Boulevard represents the cultural heart of Flushing Chinatown. Flushing's rise as the largest epicenter of Chinese culture outside Asia has been attributed to the remarkable diversity of regional Chinese demographics represented. The growth of the business activity at the core of Downtown Flushing, dominated by the Flushing Chinatown, has continued to flourish despite the COVID-19 pandemic.{{cite web|url=https://www.curbed.com/2022/12/new-new-york-report-review-hochul-adams-doctoroff.html|title=Can the Hochul-Adams New New York Actually Happen?|first=Justin | last = Davidson |work=[[Curbed]] | publisher = [[New York (magazine)}New York magazine]] |date=December 15, 2022|access-date=December 18, 2022}} The former Flushing Mall, a [[shopping center]] known for its Asian [[food court]], closed in January 2015 and was subsequently redeveloped.{{cite news |last=Chang |first=Chris |title=Flushing: NYC's 'hot' Chinatown |url=https://usa.chinadaily.com.cn/epaper/2015-05/15/content_20725206.htm |work=China Daily USA |date=May 15, 2015 |access-date=August 25, 2026}} ====Languages==== Many languages are spoken in Flushing Chinatown. English can be heard alongside many [[Sinitic languages]], such as various [[Mandarin Chinese|Mandarin]] ([[Northeastern Mandarin]], [[Beijing dialect]]),{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/10/22/nyregion/22chinese.html|title=In Chinatown, Sound of the Future Is Mandarin|date=2009-10-21|access-date=2011-07-16 | work=The New York Times | first=Kirk | last=Semple }} [[Min Chinese|Min]] ([[Fuzhou dialect|Fuzhounese]], [[Hokkien]]), [[Wu Chinese|Wu]] ([[Shanghainese]], [[Suzhou dialect|Suzhounese]], [[Hangzhou dialect|Hangzhounese]], [[Wenzhou dialect|Wenzhounese]]) and [[Cantonese]], while [[Hakka Chinese|Hakka]] varieties and [[Mongolian language|Mongolian]] are now emerging. ====Cuisine==== The most popular styles of [[Chinese cuisine]] are accessible in Flushing,{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/07/30/dining/30flushing.html|title=Let the Meals Begin: Finding Beijing in Flushing|first=Julia|last=Moskin|work=The New York Times|date=2008-07-30|access-date=2011-06-26}} including [[Korean-Chinese cuisine]], [[Hakka cuisine|Hakka]], [[Taiwanese cuisine|Taiwanese]], [[Shanghai cuisine|Shanghainese]], [[Hunan cuisine|Hunanese]], [[Sichuan cuisine|Sichuanese]], [[Cantonese cuisine|Cantonese]], [[Fujianese cuisine|Fujianese]], [[Xinjiang cuisine|Xinjiang]], and [[Zhejiang cuisine]]. Even the relatively obscure [[Northeastern Chinese cuisine|Dongbei]] style of cuisine indigenous to [[Northeast China]] is now available in Flushing,{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2010/02/10/dining/10chine.html|title=Northeast China Branches Out in Flushing|date=2010-02-09|access-date=2011-05-09| work=The New York Times | first=Julia | last=Moskin}} as well as [[Mongolian cuisine]] and [[Uyghur cuisine]].{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2018/08/25/dining/food-queens-us-open.html|title=A World of Food, Outside the U.S. Open Gates |first=Max | last = Falkowitz|newspaper=The New York Times|date=August 25, 2018|access-date=August 25, 2018}} These diverse Chinese immigrant populations have brought with them their own regional food cuisines which have led to Flushing being considered the "food mecca" for [[Chinese regional cuisine]] outside of Asia.{{cite web|url=https://ny.eater.com/2018/3/13/17085910/tianjin-chinese-flushing-nyc|title=A Look at Tianjin Cuisine, Northern Chinese Fare Found in Flushing|website=eater.com|last=Sietsema|first=Robert|date=13 March 2018|access-date=April 14, 2018}}{{cite web|url=https://www.villagevoice.com/2017/11/03/in-flushing-a-beacon-for-northeastern-chinese-cuisine-shines-bright/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171103211847/https://www.villagevoice.com/2017/11/03/in-flushing-a-beacon-for-northeastern-chinese-cuisine-shines-bright/|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 3, 2017|title=In Flushing, A Beacon for Northeastern Chinese Cuisine Shines Bright | first = Zachary | last = Feldman |date=3 November 2017 |work= [[The Village Voice]] | publisher = Village Voice, LLC |access-date=April 14, 2018}} ====Media==== The ''[[World Journal]]'', one of the largest Chinese-language newspapers outside China, is headquartered in adjacent [[Whitestone, Queens|Whitestone]], Queens, with offices in Flushing as well. Numerous other Chinese newspapers such as the ''[[China Press]]'', ''[[Sing Tao Daily]]'', ''[[The Epoch Times]]'', as well as other English-language publications, are available in the Flushing Chinatown. [[SinoVision]], one of the largest Chinese-speaking media networks in North America, also has headquarters in Flushing. ====Educational centers==== In accompaniment with its rapid growth, Flushing in particular has witnessed the proliferation of highly competitive businesses touted as educational centers{{cite magazine|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2017/10/25/magazine/asian-test-prep-centers-offer-parents-exactly-what-they-want-results.html|title=Asian Test-Prep Centers Offer Parents Exactly What They Want: 'Results'|first=Alice | last = Yin|magazine=The New York Times Magazine|date=October 25, 2017|access-date=October 26, 2017}} as well as non-profit organizations declaring the intent to educate the community. Some entities offer education in [[Standard Chinese|Mandarin]],{{cite news|url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/fullpage.html?res=9D04E3D61730F93BA15756C0A9619C8B63&sec=&spon=&&scp=2&sq=mandarin%20classes%20flushing&st=cse|title=In Queens, Classes in Mandarin Are Also Lessons in Adaptation|date=2007-05-28|access-date=2010-04-03 | work=The New York Times | first=Ellen | last=Barry}} the [[lingua franca]] of Mainland China; others profess to provide students with intensive training in computer and technological proficiency; while still others entice high school students with rigorous preparatory classes for college entrance examinations in mathematics, science, and English literacy (see: [[cram school]] and [[buxiban]]). ===Public institutions and services=== [[File:Queens Library, Flushing, June 19, 2025.jpg|thumb|250px|A branch of the [[Queens Public Library]] in Flushing Chinatown.]] The largest of the Flushing branches of the [[Queens Borough Public Library]] is located at the intersection of Kissena Boulevard and Main Street.{{cite web|url=https://www.queenslibrary.org/about-us/locations/flushing|title=Flushing|publisher=[[Queens Public Library]]|access-date=2012-02-23}} This library houses an auditorium for public events. New York Hospital Queens, a member of the [[NewYork-Presbyterian Healthcare System]],{{cite web |url=http://www.nyhq.org/|title=About the Hospital | publisher = New York Hospital Queens |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20101127154246/http://nyhq.org/About_the_Hospital |archive-date=November 27, 2010}} is a major medical center providing Flushing as well as surrounding communities with comprehensive [[health care|medical care]] services. Numerous [[health care#Tertiary care|tertiary medical clinics]] also serve the residents of Flushing. A diverse array of social services geared toward assisting recent as well as established [[Chinese immigrants]] is readily available in Flushing.{{cite web|url=https://a069-webapps3.nyc.gov/dsial/Agency_Detail.aspx?id=196 |title=Chinese Immigrants Services, Inc. | date = 2006 | work = Mayor's Office of Immigrant Affairs | publisher = The City of New York |access-date=April 7, 2010 |url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100527150443/https://a069-webapps3.nyc.gov/dsial/Agency_Detail.aspx?id=196|archive-date=2010-05-27}} ===Transportation=== The [[New York City Subway]]'s {{NYCS trains|Flushing}} has its terminus at [[Flushing – Main Street (IRT Flushing Line)|Flushing – Main Street]]; the intersection of Main Street and Roosevelt Avenue, at the heart of Flushing Chinatown, is the third busiest intersection in New York City, behind only [[Times Square]] and [[Herald Square]] in Manhattan. It is the busiest subway station in Queens and the 12th busiest station overall {{as of|2016}}.{{NYCS const|riderref}} Numerous other public bus and rail connections also serve Chinatown at the Main Street/Roosevelt Avenue intersection, including 22 [[MTA Regional Bus Operations|bus routes]] operated by [[New York City Bus]], [[MTA Bus]], and [[NICE Bus|NICE]] Bus, as well as the [[Port Washington Branch]] of the [[Long Island Rail Road]].{{cite web|url=http://www.mta.info/nyct/service/sevenlin.htm|title=MTA/New York City Transit Subway Line Information - Flushing-Main Street/Roosevelt Avenue | work = MTA.info | publisher = [[Metropolitan Transportation Authority]] |access-date=April 15, 2010|archive-date=April 3, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140403055847/http://www.mta.info/nyct/service/sevenlin.htm|url-status=dead}} Flushing Chinatown is also readily accessible by automobile from several major highways, namely the [[Grand Central Parkway]] and the [[Whitestone Expressway]]/[[Van Wyck Expressway]]. There are also multiple [[dollar van]] services shuttling passengers between Flushing Chinatown and the other Chinatowns in New York City and Long Island. ===Political clout=== The political stature of Flushing Chinatown appears to be increasing significantly. [[Taiwan]]-born [[John Liu]], former [[New York City Council]] member representing District 20, which includes Flushing Chinatown and other northern Queens neighborhoods, was elected [[New York City Comptroller]] in November 2009. Concomitantly, [[Peter Koo]], born in [[Shanghai]], China was elected to succeed Liu to assume this council membership seat. === Controversy === In March 2019, ''The New York Times'' reported that the Flushing Chinatown has also become the epicenter of [[Prostitution|organized prostitution]] in the United States, importing women from China, Korea, Thailand, and Eastern Europe to sustain the underground North American [[sex trade]].{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/03/02/us/massage-parlors-human-trafficking.html|title=Behind Illicit Massage Parlors Lie a Vast Crime Network and Modern Indentured Servitude|last1=Kulish|first1=Nicholas|date=2019-03-02|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-12-27|last2=Robles|first2=Frances|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331|last3=Mazzei|first3=Patricia}} ==Satellite Chinatowns== ===Chinatown in Elmhurst=== [[File:Bwy Elmhurst Chinatown jeh.jpg|thumb|left|250px|The Elmhurst Chinatown on Broadway, a satellite of Flushing Chinatown.]] [[Elmhurst, Queens#Chinatown|Elmhurst's rapidly growing Chinatown]]{{cite web|url=http://queens.about.com/od/photogalleries/ig/Photos-of-Elmhurst/Elmhurst-Chinatown-.htm |title=A Growing Chinatown in Elmhurst: East and Southeast Asian businesses along Broadway | first = John | last = Roleke | work = About.com | access-date=October 1, 2010 |archive-date=July 11, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140711032947/http://queens.about.com/od/photogalleries/ig/Photos-of-Elmhurst/Elmhurst-Chinatown-.htm|url-status=dead}} is the second in Queens, in addition to the Flushing Chinatown. Previously a small area with Chinese shops on [[Broadway (Queens)|Broadway]] between 81st Street and Cornish Avenue, this newly evolved second Chinatown in Queens has now expanded to 45th Avenue and Whitney Avenue and is developing as a satellite of the Flushing Chinatown. There are also many other [[Southeast Asia]]n businesses and shops in the area, including [[Malaysian Chinese]], [[Chinese Singaporean|Singaporean Chinese]], [[Indonesian people|Indonesian]], [[Thai people|Thai]], and [[Vietnamese people|Vietnamese]]. [[Hong Kong Supermarket]] and New York Supermarket serve as the largest Chinese supermarkets selling different food varieties to this Elmhurst Chinatown.{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=YjJSI1L5QCQC&q=Hong+Kong+Supermarket+Flushing&pg=PA79|title=Nosh New York|isbn=9780312304171|access-date=12 April 2016|last1=Alperson|first1=Myra|date=20 September 2003|publisher=Macmillan }}{{cite news| url=http://cityroom.blogs.nytimes.com/2008/12/09/supermarket-to-pay-back-wages-and-overtime/ | work=The New York Times | first=Steven | last=Greenhouse | title=Supermarket to Pay Back Wages and Overtime | date=December 9, 2008}} [[Financial institution]]s have emerged along Broadway to serve the various Chinese communities of Elmhurst. Like Flushing's Chinatown, it is also very highly populated by Mandarin speakers, although many also speak other languages like Hakka. ===Chinese enclave in Corona=== An annexation of the Elmhurst Chinatown is the neighborhood of [[Corona, Queens|Corona]], emerging as a Chinatown geographically connecting the larger Chinatowns in Flushing and Elmhurst. ===Chinese enclave in Whitestone=== [[File:World Journal Whitestone jeh.JPG|thumb|250px|The ''[[World Journal]]'', the largest Chinese-language newspaper in the United States and one of the largest Chinese-language newspapers outside of China, with a daily circulation of 350,000, is headquartered in [[Whitestone, Queens|Whitestone]], Queens, with offices in the adjacent Flushing Chinatown as well."[http://www.worldjournal.com/contact_us-e Contact Us] ([http://www.worldjournal.com/contact_us Page in Chinese]) World Journal. Retrieved on 2014-10-03. "New York Headquarters 141-07 20th Ave. Whitestone, NY 11357"]]Since 2000, thousands of [[Chinese American]]s have migrated into [[Whitestone, Queens|Whitestone]], given the sizeable presence of the neighboring Flushing Chinatown, and have continued their expansion eastward in Queens and into neighboring, highly educated [[Nassau County, New York|Nassau County]] on [[Long Island]], which has become the leading suburban destination in the U.S. for Chinese.{{cite magazine|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/hengshao/2014/04/10/chinese-real-estate-buyers-fan-out-to-long-islands-north-shore/|title=Join The Great Gatsby: Chinese Real Estate Buyers Fan Out To Long Island's North Shore|author=Heng Shao|magazine=Forbes|date=2014-04-10|access-date=2014-10-03}}{{cite web|url=https://www.reuters.com/article/us-realestate-china-manhattan-insight-idUSBREA3O0TL20140425|title=The Chinese take Manhattan: replace Russians as top apartment buyers|first1=Michelle | last1 = Conlin | first2 = Maggie Lu | last2 = Yueyang|publisher=Thomson Reuters|date= April 25, 2014 |access-date= November 28, 2014}} The ''[[World Journal]]'', the largest Chinese-language newspaper in the United States{{cite web|url=https://www.bloomberg.com/news/2014-10-27/one-percenters-drop-six-figures-at-long-island-mall.html|title=One Percenters Drop Six Figures at Long Island Mall |first=Carol | last = Hymowitz|publisher= Bloomberg L.P. |date=October 27, 2014 |access-date=October 27, 2014}} and one of the largest Chinese-language newspapers outside China, with a daily circulation of 350,000, is headquartered in Whitestone. The New York office of [[Hong Kong]]-based [[Lee Kum Kee|Lee Kum Kee International Holdings Ltd.]] is also located in Whitestone.{{cite web | url = http://usa.lkk.com/Us/Enterprise/SalesContact/ContactUs | title = Contact Us Around the World | url-status = dead | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140812125451/http://usa.lkk.com/Us/Enterprise/SalesContact/ContactUs | archive-date=August 12, 2014 | publisher = [[Lee Kum Kee]] USA | access-date = October 3, 2014 | quote = 30-56 Whitestone Expressway, Suite #350, Whitestone, NY 11354 USA }} ===Wealthy Chinatown in Long Island City=== Since the 2020s, there has also been a rapidly growing Chinese enclave in [[Long Island City#Long Island City Chinatown/Asiatown|Long Island City]], composed mainly of higher-income residents;{{cite web |date=2026-01-25 |title=A new Chinatown emerges among the glass towers of Long Island City |url=https://www.wnyc.org/story/a-new-chinatown-emerges-among-the-glass-towers-of-long-island-city/ |access-date=2026-04-25 |website=WNYC}}{{cite news |last=Hong |first=Nicole |date=2021-10-18 |title=Inside the N.Y.C. Neighborhood With the Fastest Growing Asian Population |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2021/10/18/nyregion/long-island-city-asian-population.html |access-date=2026-04-25 |work=New York Times |page= |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}} this community was described in ''LIC Journal'' as "New York's newest Chinatown".{{cite web |last=Sinanian |first=Cole |date=2026-02-05 |title=LIC Chinatown Might Be NYC's Ritziest |url=https://www.licjournal.com/lic-chinatown-might-be-nycs-ritziest/ |access-date=2026-04-25 |website=LIC Journal}} The expanding Chinese enclave was part of a larger trend of growth in the community's Asian population, which was 34% Asian by 2021. Most of the new Asian residents in Long Island City are East Asian, specifically Chinese, Korean, or Japanese, and are second- or third-generation Americans. These residents have largely moved to the [[Luxury apartment|luxury housing developments]] that were built in the neighborhood in Long Island City, and some preschools and restaurants have been added for the growing population. On the other side of Long Island City, the [[Queensbridge Houses]] public-housing development has also been receiving working class Asian residents, with many of them being Chinese. ==See also== {{Portal|China|Hong Kong|Malaysia|New York (state)|New York City|Singapore|Taiwan|Thailand|United States|Vietnam}} * [[Long Island#Demographics|Long Island]] '''Chinatowns:''' * [[Chinatown]] * [[Chinese Americans in New York City]] * [[Chinatowns in Brooklyn]] * [[Chinatown, Manhattan]] * [[Mott Street|Little Hong Kong/Guangdong]] * [[Little Fuzhou]] * [[Avenue U#Chinatown (唐人街, U大道)|Chinatown, Avenue U]] * [[Bensonhurst#Little Hong Kong/Little Guangdong|Chinatown, Bensonhurst]] * [[New Dorp, Staten Island#Staten Island Chinatown Emerging|New Dorp, Staten Island]] * [[Chinatowns in Canada and the United States]] * [[List of Chinatowns in the United States]] '''Koreatowns:''' * [[Koreatown]] * [[Koreatown, Manhattan]] * [[Koreatown, Long Island]] * [[Koreatown, Fort Lee]] * [[Koreatown, Palisades Park]] == References == {{reflist}} {{navboxes|list= {{Flushing, Queens}} {{Queens}} {{Ethnicity in New York City}} {{US Chinatowns}} }} {{coord|40.7422|N|73.8786|W|source:wikidata-and-enwiki-cat-tree_region:US|display=title}} [[Category:Chinatowns in New York City|*Queens]] [[Category:Neighborhoods in Queens, New York]] [[Category:Flushing, Queens]] [[Category:Elmhurst, Queens]] [[Category:Corona, Queens]] [[Category:Whitestone, Queens]]
